title: Japan's Meiji Leap

cards.h: Four black ships, and a country changed in 15 years
cards.b:
In July 1853, American warships under Commodore Matthew Perry sailed into Edo Bay. They were steam-powered and painted black. Japan, closed to most outsiders for over 200 years, now had to decide.

It chose to change faster than any big country had.
The Tokugawa shogunate looked weak. Young samurai from Satsuma and Choshu rebelled. In 1868 they 'restored' the young Emperor Meiji (aged 15) to power.

The new government abolished the old feudal domains (1871), ended samurai privileges, created a conscript army (1873), built railways (first line 1872), set up schools and factories. The Iwakura Mission (1871-73) toured the US and Europe to learn.

A Constitution came in 1889, with an elected Diet but strong powers for the emperor.

Many samurai lost their income. In 1877 Saigo Takamori, once a hero of the Restoration, led the Satsuma Rebellion. Modern conscript soldiers crushed it.

It made clear that the old order was gone.

Japan beat China in the First Sino-Japanese War (1894-95) and took Taiwan. In 1902 it allied with Britain. In 1904-05 it defeated Russia, the first time an Asian power beat a European great power in a modern war.

Japan then annexed Korea (1910), becoming an imperial power itself.

Myth: a backward country suddenly woke up.Fact: Edo Japan already had big cities (Edo was among the largest in the world), high literacy for the time, banking and trade. Meiji leaders built on that.

Also, 'Restoration' was partly a slogan; the real power was held by a small group of ex-samurai officials.

Five things to remember

  1. Perry arrived in 1853; the Meiji Restoration came in 1868.
  2. Reforms: army, schools, railways, constitution (1889).
  3. The Satsuma Rebellion (1877) ended samurai power.
  4. Japan beat China (1895) and Russia (1905).
  5. 1905 inspired Indian nationalists.

Think about it

  • Why did Japan change when China resisted?
  • Can rapid modernisation have a dark side?

sources: Jansen, The Making of Modern Japan (2000); Beasley, The Meiji Restoration; Nehru, An Autobiography (1936)
